newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt moves on Zaire concern, iridium firms.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt moves on Zaire concern, iridium firms.

text.p: Cobalt, against the backdrop of war-torn Zaire, held the spotlight in minor industrial metals trading over the past week, European traders said.
Elsewhere Japanese demand lifted iridium, while its over stocked sister platinum group metal (PGM) rhodium came under pressure and was expected to fall further according to several traders.
Cobalt firmed following a U.N. statement that Eastern Zaire insurgents were advancing towards the cobalt producing belt in Shaba province.
Zaire said on Wednesday thousands of Ugandan troops had invaded its territory including one group heading for Shaba but Uganda immediately dismissed the accusation.
Zaire produces many grades of cobalt with an annual production of around 5,000 tonnes a year.
"Around 1,000 tonnes of high grade material (used in superalloys for the aerospace industry) is produced by Zaire...the rest is of lower grade metal," one trader said.
Several traders said the unrest in Zaire could have the potential to lift cobalt prices higher.
One suggested high grade material could reach $30 per pound over the coming weeks.
But others agreeing that prices would firm short-term said the market, despite booming demand from the aerospace industry, would remain in good supply.
According to the Cobalt Development Institute there is a consensus within the industry that supply from old and new sources has and will increase, even in the shortest term.
Also on Wednesday European minor metals traders said workers at Zaire cobalt and copper producer Gecamines were on strike.
They said Gecamines workers, along with many other workers in Zaire, began a protest last week over the introduction of new bank notes.
Gecamines was not available for comment, but a source close to the major cobalt producer believed output was continuing at a reduced rate.
Other traders said the market had the potential to climb against the backdrop of the political chaos and bloodshed within Zaire.
"Its a hard way to mark the price up," one trader said, but added the market had to follow fundamentals.
"If the fighting hits Shaba cobalt production will drop to zero," one trader said.
High grade cobalt was at around $22 a lb, slightly up on last weeks levels.

Platinum group metals (PGM's) iridium and rhodium moved in opposite directions in brisk trading over the last week, a condition that was showing few signs of slowing according to several European traders.
Iridium against the backdrop of Japanese demand rallied, while an overstocked rhodium market continued to spiral lower.
Traders said iridium had the potential to climb to $250 an ounce, while rhodium presently trading under $200 an ounce could tumble further to $150 near term.
"The two markets are poles apart and are following fundamentals," one trader said.
Commenting on rhodium one senior European trader said that the market was suffering from a poor structure.
Another trader said rhodium was in oversupply and added that major car producers which had used the metal for catalytic converters had turned to other alternatives.
This included the use of iridium by one Japanese car manufacturer, traders added.
The fast approaching Lunar New Year in China saw the antimony market slow. But one influential source in Europe said business was brisk.
The longs and shorts of the market continued to battle within the antimony arena.

Some suggested the higher prices recently had dampened enthusiasm to trade and believed the market was in oversupply. The other side of the coin said the high prices was sucking in consumers fearful of further price rises.
Gallium remained firm and was looking towards higher levels. Traders said the use of gallium in communication satellites was helping to fly the price higher.
Low stocks of vanadium continued to bolster prices, while titanium was also stable at higher levels againt the backdrop of aerospace demand
